title: What the KL term does to the codes
sub: A linear VAE where the best encoder can be computed exactly, at four values of β.
legend: q(z | x) for each data point

frames.caption: Six data points, each encoded as a distribution over a one-dimensional latent z (thin blue curves). Their average is the aggregate posterior (orange); the dashed curve is the prior N(0, 1) we will sample from. With β ≈ 0 there is almost no KL penalty, so each code shrinks to a spike: a plain autoencoder. Sampling z from the prior mostly lands in the gaps between spikes, where the decoder was never trained.
β = 0.3: the KL term starts to bite. Each code widens, and is pulled towards the origin.

β = 1, the true ELBO. Each encoder distribution is now the exact posterior p(z | x) (this decoder is linear, so the optimum is known in closed form). The codes are wider and touch their neighbours, and the aggregate posterior roughly follows the prior. With only six points it is bumpy, but averaged over the full data distribution it would equal the prior exactly, so samples from the prior land where the decoder has seen data.

β = 6, a β-VAE: the KL penalty dominates. Codes crowd towards N(0, 1) and overlap heavily, so z carries less information about x and reconstructions get worse. Push β far enough and every code becomes the prior itself: posterior collapse, where z says nothing about x.
